title: Symmetry obsessions with time-consuming compulsions: obsessive-compulsive disorder
vignette: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother due to unusual behavior over the past year. The mother is concerned that her daughter seems overly anxious about eating, and says, "During lunch, she spent 45 minutes cutting the broccoli on her plate until all the pieces were the same size." The patient recently became a vegetarian and spends hours in the grocery store selecting vegetables and checking nutritional information. She also seems very concerned about her appearance; she brushes her hair 21 times on each side, parts her hair strand by strand, and plucks her eyebrows for an hour daily. The patient says, "If I don't keep things exactly even I'm afraid something bad might happen." The patient is medically healthy and has not yet started menstruating. She weighs 45.8 kg (101 lb) and is 157.5 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall. BMI is 18.5 kg/m2. Physical examination is normal with the exception of extremely sparse eyebrows. Which of the following is the most likely primary diagnosis?

clues.text: cutting the broccoli on her plate until all the pieces were the same size
clues.note: Repetitive, ritualized behavior to achieve exactness/symmetry is a COMPULSION.

clues.text: brushes her hair 21 times on each side, parts her hair strand by strand
clues.note: Time-consuming, rule-bound grooming rituals are compulsions performed in response to an obsession with symmetry.

clues.text: If I don't keep things exactly even I'm afraid something bad might happen
clues.note: A persistent, intrusive fear (obsession) driving repetitive behaviors to prevent a feared outcome defines OCD.

whatMatters: Persistent, intrusive obsessions (symmetry/exactness; a feared bad outcome) plus time-consuming, ritualized COMPULSIONS (cutting food evenly, counting hair strokes, plucking) that the patient feels driven to perform = OBSESSIVE-COMPULSIVE DISORDER. Answer D.
strategy: Identify obsessions (intrusive symmetry thoughts, magical fear) and compulsions (repetitive rituals to neutralize them) that are time-consuming/distressing = OCD. Reject anorexia nervosa (normal BMI 18.5 for age; behaviors are symmetry-driven, not fear of weight gain), body dysmorphic disorder (preoccupation with a perceived appearance DEFECT), generalized anxiety disorder (excessive worry about many issues, no compulsions), obsessive-compulsive PERSONALITY disorder (pervasive perfectionism/control WITHOUT true obsessions/compulsions; not diagnosed in adolescents), and trichotillomania (hair-pulling as the primary disorder, not driven by a symmetry obsession).

eliminations.label: Anorexia nervosa - normal BMI, not weight-fear driven
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: restriction/low body weight from intense fear of weight gain and distorted body image. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: her BMI (18.5) is normal for age/sex and her food behaviors are driven by SYMMETRY obsessions, not fear of gaining weight. ✅ Correct if: significantly low weight with fear of weight gain/body-image distortion.

eliminations.label: Body dysmorphic disorder - perceived appearance defect
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: preoccupation with a perceived physical DEFECT. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: her rituals aim to prevent a feared event via symmetry, not to fix a specific perceived flaw. ✅ Correct if: obsessive focus on a specific 'defect' with mirror-checking.

eliminations.label: Generalized anxiety disorder - worry, no compulsions
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: excessive worry about multiple life domains. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: GAD lacks intrusive obsessions and ritualized compulsions; this patient has both. ✅ Correct if: chronic multi-domain worry without compulsions.

eliminations.label: OC personality disorder - perfectionism without obsessions/compulsions
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a lifelong pattern of orderliness, control, and perfectionism (ego-syntonic). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: OCPD lacks true obsessions/compulsions, is generally not diagnosed before 18, and wouldn't explain her recurrent rituals driven by intrusive fears. ✅ Correct if: pervasive perfectionism/rigidity without discrete obsessions/compulsions.

eliminations.label: Trichotillomania - hair-pulling as primary disorder
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: recurrent hair-pulling with attempts to stop (a body-focused repetitive behavior). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: her eyebrow-plucking is part of a broader symmetry-obsession/compulsion pattern, so OCD is the primary diagnosis. ✅ Correct if: isolated hair-pulling without obsessions.

reasoning: The patient has intrusive obsessions (symmetry/exactness; fear that something bad will happen)
She performs time-consuming compulsions (cutting food evenly, counting hair strokes, plucking) to neutralize them
This pattern is distressing/time-consuming and ego-dystonic = OCD
mechanism: OBSESSIVE-COMPULSIVE DISORDER (OCD) is defined by OBSESSIONS - recurrent, intrusive, unwanted, anxiety-provoking thoughts, urges, or images - and/or COMPULSIONS - repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed to reduce the anxiety or to prevent a feared (often magically connected) outcome. To qualify, the obsessions/compulsions must be TIME-CONSUMING (>1 hour/day) or cause significant DISTRESS or functional IMPAIRMENT; OCD is typically chronic and begins in childhood/adolescence. This patient's SYMMETRY/exactness obsessions ('if I don't keep things even, something bad might happen') drive ritualized COMPULSIONS (cutting food into equal pieces for 45 minutes, brushing hair a set number of times per side, meticulous grooming). Treatment is an SSRI and/or cognitive-behavioral therapy (exposure and response prevention). The behaviors are NOT explained by anorexia (normal BMI; not weight-fear driven), body dysmorphic disorder (perceived defect), generalized anxiety (no compulsions), OC personality disorder (perfectionism without true obsessions/compulsions, not diagnosed in a 14-year-old), or trichotillomania (isolated hair-pulling).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Psych > OCD: obsessions (intrusive thoughts) + compulsions (ritualized behaviors to reduce anxiety/prevent feared event); time-consuming (>1 h/day) or impairing; onset childhood/adolescence; treat SSRI + CBT (exposure/response prevention); ego-dystonic (vs ego-syntonic OCPD).

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Symmetry obsessions + time-consuming rituals to prevent a feared event = OCD.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on obsession vs compulsion, ego-dystonic vs ego-syntonic, OCD vs OCPD, or body dysmorphic disorder? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Anorexia = weight fear/low BMI; BDD = perceived defect; GAD = worry no compulsions; OCPD = perfectionism (no obsessions); trichotillomania = isolated hair-pulling.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: OCD = obsessions + compulsions, time-consuming/distressing; treat SSRI + CBT (ERP); ego-dystonic.

keywords.back: OCD = ego-dystonic obsessions/compulsions; OCPD = ego-syntonic perfectionism
Preoccupation with a perceived appearance defect

firstAid.detail: Psych > anorexia, BDD, GAD, OCPD, trichotillomania.

memoryHook: Intrusive 'keep it even or something bad happens' thoughts fueling hours of evening-up rituals = OCD (the thoughts feel wrong to her - ego-dystonic).
